doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

title: Leaving a formal school and studying with Art Perretta
summary: Unhappy at a formal school, he studies about three years with Art Perretta in Hartford, who gives classical training.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Good point. Very prevalent around here unfortunately. So did you continue your education in a more formal setting?

Yes I did. I went to a very formal school that we’ll just omit the name, and started to study there, and was not happy at all with the teaching staff and the direction I was going. Of course I had been out and playing, and I knew what I needed. I just wasn’t at their beck and call. I knew what I needed, and they weren’t giving it to me. So I pulled out of the school and started asking successful drummers and musicians about a good communicator. Not only a good player, but someone that could communicate that knowledge. And I found a gentlemen, Art Perretta, in Hartford, who was teaching at the Hartford Conservatory. And I studied with him for about three years. And he gave me classical training, taught me how to read, a wonderful teacher, and again a big influence, and a very mild mannered man, and also instilled some of that into me too, and how to interact with other musicians on and off the bandstand. And I think my worst lesson with him was I finished playing a book and he closed it, and he says, “Gregory, I can do no more for you.” And it left such an impact because I had such respect for this man. He says, “You need to go on with another teacher.” And I did.
It was. I gave him a hug and still keep in contact with him to this day, and he with me.
The instructors at this school that you choose not to mention, do you think the problem was were the teachers there more academiacs — is that a word?

Maybe, but I know what you mean. I have to say yes. Literally putting in time and not taking a personal side to teaching, really analyzing what the students need, and looking at the clock, your half hour’s up, things of that nature. I just wasn’t happy with that. Dedication, not there.
